analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test their AI decision systems for bias, accuracy, and privacy risks before using them.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring large companies to study their automated decision systems — like the algorithms that decide who gets a loan, a job interview, or an apartment — for accuracy, bias, discrimination, and privacy risks, and to fix the problems they find [S2][S3]. It applied only to bigger companies, those over $50 million in annual revenue or holding data on more than a million people, plus data brokers [S3]. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules [S3]. It was never considered beyond being referred to committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers — anyone evaluated by an algorithm for credit, employment, housing, insurance, or pricing, and anyone whose personal data sits in large corporate databases. The assessments would have checked whether these systems make inaccurate, unfair, biased, or discriminatory decisions about people, covering sensitive categories like race, health, genetics, and religion [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers judged by automated decision systems

how_it_helps.text: Companies would have had to examine their algorithms' design and training data for impacts on accuracy, fairness, bias, discrimination, privacy, and security, and take steps to minimize the risks found [S3].

The rules cover systems that predict sensitive aspects of people's lives — work performance, economic situation, health, location — and systems handling large amounts of personal data on race, religion, health, criminal convictions, and other protected categories [S3].
Assessments of new high-risk systems would be required before the system is put into use, not after harm has occurred [S3].
Enforcement would fall to the FTC as an unfair-or-deceptive-practices matter and to state attorneys general, and the bill explicitly does not preempt stronger state laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large tech companies, data brokers, and any firm over $50 million in revenue or holding data on more than a million consumers, which would bear the cost of impact assessments, outside auditors, and fixing biased or insecure systems. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech firms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The assessments do not have to be made public — a covered entity may publish them 'at its sole discretion' — so the accountability rests on regulators rather than transparency to consumers [S3].
The bill creates no right for individual consumers to sue over a biased algorithm; relief depends on FTC and state attorney general action [S3].

Compliance costs — studies, external auditors, redesigning systems — fall on companies and could be passed through to consumers in prices, and critics of algorithm-audit mandates argue they can slow useful products while rarely catching subtle discrimination.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: checking the systems that gate people's access to credit, jobs, housing, and insurance for bias and errors before they are deployed. The design has honest weaknesses — results stay private unless the company chooses to publish, and individuals cannot sue — but the thresholds exempt small businesses, so costs concentrate on large firms that profit from the data. On balance the public benefit outweighs the compliance cost, and the bill died without that tradeoff ever being debated.

outcome.mechanism: After introduction, the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which never took it up before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on April 10, 2019, with Sen. Cory Booker joining as the original cosponsor [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S5].
The bill's only recorded action beyond the referral is none; it attracted a single cosponsor and never reached a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use or sell automated decision systems and personal data — large tech platforms and data brokers — are better off because the assessment requirements never took effect and they avoided the audit, disclosure, and redesign costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tech firms and data brokers that avoided audits

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker

for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only Democratic sponsorship — two senators total — and no Republican or industry action on the bill, so no partisan split was ever tested with a vote.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and AI/algorithm vendors
industries.note: The bill would have forced companies over $50 million in revenue or holding data on more than a million people to audit their automated decision systems for bias, accuracy, and privacy risks before deployment, with FTC and state enforcement [S3]. Their interest in avoiding those audits and potential redesign costs runs against consumers' interest in fair, accurate decisions [S3].

Data brokers are covered by definition regardless of size, and would have had to conduct data protection impact assessments on systems handling personal information [S3]. Their business model — assembling and selling data on people who are not their customers — is precisely what the assessments scrutinize.
